parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Your task now is to interview one future user and find out what they need. You will not see any other description of their work: what you learn, you learn from them.

What you know about the business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The users of the future service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You are now interviewing: a dispatcher. You will interview each of the other roles separately.

Cover at least these topics, in your own words and in whatever order the conversation allows:

- an ordinary working day, from start to end;
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad;
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it;
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong;
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong;
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them.

How to interview:

- Ask one question at a time. Keep questions short and open.
- Follow up wherever an answer is vague, general, or surprising. Ask for a concrete example.
- Do not suggest answers, features, or solutions, and do not describe how the service could work.
- Do not summarise the interview back to the interviewee.
- You can ask at most 30 questions in this interview.
- When every topic is covered and follow-ups no longer bring anything new, end by writing exactly `END OF INTERVIEW` on its own line, and nothing else in that message.

Write only your next question.
The interviewee is ready. Ask your first question.
Could you start by telling me which company you work for, and walking me through what an ordinary shift looks like for you from start to finish?

I work as a dispatcher at one of the drone operating companies that uses the platform's shared service. My job involves planning and running flights, which means I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can also call off a flight. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and several dispatchers plan while closures can come into force even while drones of several companies are already in the air.
Where do the flight requests come from at the start of your day, and who do you hand work off to once you've planned or completed a flight?
I don't know.
When you plan and run a flight, how do you interact with the fleet technicians or the airspace desk?
I don't know.

[-Thinking-]
 Let's follow up on what the user mentioned in the first answer: "Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones" and "Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and several dispatchers plan while closures can come into force even while drones of several companies are already in the air." Let's ask about the worst day of the last few months.
[/-Thinking-]What has been your worst day at work over the last few months, and what made it so bad?
I don't know.

[-Thinking-]
The interviewee says "I don't know" to general questions not matching their specific knowledge base. Let's look at the first answer carefully and probe the things they *did* mention, while also hitting the required topics.
In the first answer, they said:
- "I decide which drone flies along which way, and I sign off a flight before it leaves."
- "Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I can also call off a flight."
- "Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and several dispatchers plan while closures can come into force even while drones of several companies are already in the air."

Let's ask about what goes wrong when several dispatchers plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, or when closures come into force.
[/-Thinking-]What happens when several dispatchers try to plan flights for the same popular drone or busy site at the same time?

I plan and run flights while several dispatchers are planning at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and closures can come into force even while drones of several companies are already in the air.

[-Thinking-]
Let's check the required topics:
- an ordinary working day, from start to end (asked)
- the worst day of the last few months, and what made it bad (asked)
- what they check by hand today because they do not trust it
- what they are afraid a new service would do wrong
- what they need to know right after something has gone wrong
- who they hand work to, and who hands work to them (asked)

Let's ask what they check by hand before signing off a flight.
[/-Thinking-]What do you currently check by hand before you sign off a flight because you don't trust it to be right otherwise?

I am the licensed person responsible for each flight, and I decide which drone flies along which way before I sign off a flight. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and closures can come into force even while drones of several companies are already in the air.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask what they are afraid a new service would do wrong.
[/-Thinking-]What are you most afraid a new service might do wrong when you are planning or running flights?

Our company policy is that software never chooses a drone or a way for us, and choosing them is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher. Several dispatchers plan at the same time, often for the same busy sites and popular drones. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and closures can come into force while drones are already in the air.

[-Thinking-]
Now let's ask what they need to know right after something has gone wrong (e.g., when something happens outside their control or a closure comes into force).
[/-Thinking-]When something goes wrong—such as a closure coming into force while drones are in the air, or something else outside your control—what do you need to know right away?

I need to know when authorities announce sudden or planned closures, which can be amended during the day and can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Things happen outside our control both before and during a flight, and radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on.

[-Thinking-]
That brought out a lot of new details! Let's follow up on patchy radio coverage, batteries draining faster, and drones restarting in flight.
[/-Thinking-]When radio coverage drops out, a drone restarts in flight, or a battery drains faster than planned, what happens on your end and what do you do?

Radio coverage is patchy around ports, industrial sites, and in bad weather, and reports from drones come through relay stations so they can arrive late, out of order, more than once, or not at all. Drones sometimes restart in flight after a software fault and carry on, while batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned. Before and during a flight, things happen outside our control, and closures can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask about what happens after a flight or after an incident—like investigations, logs, or legal responsibility, or how they check drone readiness, sites, or routes.
[/-Thinking-]Because you have legal responsibility for each flight, what information do you need to check about a drone, its battery, or the sites before you sign off?

I decide which drone flies along which way and I sign off a flight before it leaves. Batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned, and drones have a home site and various models with different battery ranges, cargo capacities, sensors, and non-interchangeable charging connectors. Sites also have a limited number of places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

[-Thinking-]
That's great information: "drones have a home site and various models with different battery ranges, cargo capacities, sensors, and non-interchangeable charging connectors. Sites also have a limited number of places where drones can take off and land at the same time."
Let's ask more about how sites, charging connectors, and maintenance/fleet status affect their flight planning.
[/-Thinking-]How do the different drone models, charging connectors, and limited takeoff and landing spots at sites affect how you plan a flight?

Drones are of several models from different manufacturers that differ in battery range, cargo capacity, sensors, and charging connectors, which are not interchangeable. Each drone has a home site with its own charging pads that are never lent to another company. Sites also have only so many places where drones can take off and land at the same time.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask about how they know if a drone is available or fit to fly, or how they coordinate with fleet technicians on maintenance and inspections.
[/-Thinking-]How do you know whether a drone is fit to fly or unavailable due to maintenance or inspection when you are planning a flight?
I don't know.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask about the "way" (route/corridor/path) and airspace closures: how do they choose a way, and how do airspace closures work?
[/-Thinking-]When you decide which way a drone flies, what makes a way valid or invalid, and how do airspace closures affect it?

Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and authorities define zones where flying is prohibited as well as announcing planned or sudden closures. These closures can be amended during the day and can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Our company policy is that software never chooses a way for us, and choosing it is my legal responsibility as a dispatcher.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask about what happens when a closure comes into force while one of their drones is already in the air, or when they call off a flight.
[/-Thinking-]What happens when you call off a flight, or when a closure comes into force while one of your drones is already flying along a corridor?

As a dispatcher, I can call off a flight, and closures can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air. Drones fly along corridors between named sites, and authorities define zones where flying is prohibited and announce planned or sudden closures. These closures are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves.

[-Thinking-]
Let's ask if there is anything else about jobs, customers, confidentiality between companies, or audit/records after a flight.
[/-Thinking-]What do you need to keep private from the other drone companies using the platform, and what is shared?
Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. We do accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.
